title: signal-vs-noise-interview-diary - Aina Ronson
content:
Purpose: quick-running, low-friction diary to capture the ephemeral gut-level signals from phone screens and early loops. Not meant for PR or panel distribution — more of an internal memory aid and heuristic store.

Context: today ran three 30m screens for Senior Runtime Engineer candidates. Jotted reactions in real time, then cleaned up. I want an explicit checklist for which signals actually predict later-stage success for our team (serving runtime): technical depth, operational intuition, shipping instincts, communication under ambiguity, and ownership over tradeoffs.

Rating sketch (quick):
 - system design clarity: 1-5
 - troubleshooting posture: 1-5
 - code ergonomics fluency (talking about abstractions): 1-5
 - product sensibility / prioritization: 1-5
 - culture fit (teamwork + curiosity): 1-5

Candidate A (phone screen 09:00) — "C. N." (anonymized)
 - system design clarity: 4
 - troubleshooting posture: 3
 - code ergonomics fluency: 4
 - product sensibility: 3
 - culture fit: 4
 Notes: strong on low-level kernel tradeoffs and quantization implications (fast, confident). Used concrete microbench numbers (latency impact of int8 vs fp16) which is useful for runtime work. Hesitant on orchestration questions (how to handle KV cache across sharded GPUs) — gave a strawman but no clear operational rollback plan.
 Quick flag: heavy on solo-coder stories; less evidence coordinating cross-team rollouts. Follow-up ask: request a short write-up (1 page) on how they'd do a rollout for a new model variant with rollback and cost controls.

Candidate B (phone screen 10:00) — "M. P."
 - system design clarity: 3
 - troubleshooting posture: 5
 - code ergonomics fluency: 3
 - product sensibility: 5
 - culture fit: 4
 Notes: super strong debugging stories — one anecdote about a memory leak across cuda streams that was diagnosed by instrumenting the allocator (excellent practical signal). Extremely comfortable asking clarifying questions and surfacing constraints (SLOs, cost, security) early. Not as deep on attention-kernel internals, but very good at triage and cross-team coordination.
 Quick flag: good site reliability instincts; would pair well with someone deep in kernel work.

Candidate C (phone screen 11:30) — "L. X."
 - system design clarity: 2
 - troubleshooting posture: 2
 - code ergonomics fluency: 2
 - product sensibility: 3
 - culture fit: 3
 Notes: nervous, long pauses. Answers tended toward hypotheticals without concrete executions. Good theoretical knowledge but limited real-world examples at scale. Asked about mentorship and growth path — seems motivated but may need more ramping.
 Quick flag: probably not a good fit for a senior IC role today; maybe a solid mid-level candidate for a two-quarter plan.

Patterns I noticed (meta):
 - Actual predictive signals: the stories where a candidate says what they measured, why they changed the approach, and what they learned (numbers + mental model) often correlate with later-stage success.
 - Weak signal: high-level buzzword descriptions of distributed caching without any mention of latencies, fallbacks, or instrumentation.
 - Strong interpersonal flag: people who volunteer to write a short doc or follow-up plan immediately after the screen show operational ownership.

Heuristics to try next week (experiments):
 - Ask each candidate to narrate one incident where a rollout failed and to sketch a concrete rollback plan (score 1-5 for completeness).
 - Add a 5-minute practical prompt: "Given an observed 30% tail-latency spike in production after a model change, what are your first 6 investigative steps?" Timebox to 5 minutes to force prioritization.
 - For kernel/infra candidates: present a tiny microbenchmark (pseudo) and have them explain what they'd measure, what noise they'd expect, and what signal would worry them.

Unresolved follow-ups (action items):
 - email candidate A asking for the rollout write-up (deadline: 2025-02-23).
 - share Candidate B's memory-leak anecdote with SRE on-call for quick calibration — likely reusable for an interview prompt.
 - file a short Linear ticket (RED-xxxx) to capture the 5-minute prompt and add it to the phone screen rubric.

Notes-to-self:
 - stop letting candidate responses drift into design-novelty land; always push for measured outcomes (what metrics moved?).
 - keep a small crib sheet of model-inference microbenchmarks (latency/cost examples) to anchor kernel conversations — candidates who can tie decisions to numbers are winners.
 - avoid over-weighting charisma; create a balanced rubric that privileges reproducible impact.

Random raw snippets (verbatim-ish):
 - Candidate B: "I instrumented the allocator and found a 40MB/epoch leak when we changed the batch-collation path." -> good
 - Candidate A: "Quantization seemed fine in my experiments" (no numbers) -> neutral / ask for numbers
 - Candidate C: extended silence on how they'd instrument a KV-cache mismatch -> red flag

Mini-rubric draft (for phone screens):
 - Measurable impact story (0-3): did they state numbers, duration, and outcome?
 - Troubleshooting flow (0-3): hypothesis -> test -> iterate?
 - Collaboration evidence (0-2): cross-team communication, docs, rollouts
 - Domain signal (0-2): domain-specific depth (kernels, batching, caching) appropriate to role

Wrap-up: consolidate notes in 24h and mark any follow-ups in Linear. Keep this diary format — low friction to update and helps reduce recency bias for panel decisions. If a candidate is borderline, weigh candidate B-style operational instincts more heavily for our early hiring needs.

---
Quick log: saved as draft in case I want to anonymize before sharing. Will add short follow-up prompts for the loop packet if any candidate advances.

End of entry.
